title: Stellantis selling refurbished high-voltage batteries - electrive.com
content:
Automobile
SUSTAINera, Stellantis' circular economy business unit, is expanding its range of refurbished parts with a focus on electric and hybrid vehicles. Refurbished high-voltage batteries are now available for most BEV and PHEV models of Stellantis brands.
Stellantis refurbishes high-voltage batteries
Image: Stellantis
SUSTAINera has made it its mission to develop solutions within the 4R strategy – Remanufacturing, Repair, Reuse, Recycle – that extend product lifespans, avoid waste, conserve resources and reduce the CO
footprint. This includes, in particular, the disassembly and refurbishment of vehicle components so they can be reused as spare parts in other cars.
SUSTAINera is now expanding its range of refurbished parts from internal combustion engine vehicles to include electric and hybrid vehicles. This covers high-voltage batteries, electrically driven compressors and electrified dual-clutch transmissions for mild hybrids. All parts are refurbished to OEM specifications, with the same performance characteristics and warranty conditions as MOPAR original parts.
According to Stellantis: refurbished spare parts are more environmentally friendly, as they save up to 80 per cent of raw materials and up to 40 per cent of CO
emissions compared to new parts – thereby supporting resource-efficient mobility. Incidentally, SUSTAINera has already supplied refurbished EV batteries for stationary energy storage systems in the past, such as
for Rome Airport
Stellantis will showcase the refurbished products next week at Automechanika in Frankfurt (8 to 12 September) in Hall 9.0, Stand F84-E84. The trade fair appearance is designed as a live workshop environment, allowing visitors to experience Stellantis’ 360° aftermarket approach firsthand. In a dedicated exhibition area, SUSTAINera will demonstrate how circular economy solutions can benefit workshops, aftermarket professionals, dealers and customers.

title: Vulcan advances Ludwig lithium project - electrive.com
content:
Vulcan Energy has presented a pre-feasibility study for its second lithium project in the Upper Rhine Valley. The Ludwigshafen region is expected to produce 21,100 tons of lithium carbonate annually. However, several development steps are still required before an investment decision can be made.
Vulcan is also building a lithium processing plant in Frankfurt-Höchst.
Image: Vulcan Energy
Vulcan Energy is advancing plans for a second lithium and geothermal project in the Upper Rhine Valley. The project, named Ludwig, will be located in the Ludwigshafen region and builds on the experience gained from the more advanced Lionheart project near Landau. The German-Australian company has now published a pre-feasibility study (PFS) for Ludwig.
Lionheart
, Vulcan intends to extract lithium-rich geothermal brine from underground while simultaneously harnessing its geothermal energy. For Ludwig, the brine will be transported to a central processing plant. There, Vulcan plans to first use its proprietary Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE) technology to produce lithium chloride, which will then be further processed on-site into battery-grade lithium carbonate. In contrast, for Lionheart, lithium extraction and processing are split between Landau and Frankfurt-Höchst.
For Ludwig, the pre-feasibility study assumes an annual production of 21,100 tonnes of lithium carbonate. Additionally, up to 3,125 GWh of renewable heat per year is expected to be generated, intended for both the company’s own production processes and regional customers. Combined with the planned 24,000 tonnes of lithium hydroxide monohydrate (LHM) from Lionheart, Vulcan estimates it will produce enough lithium for the batteries of around one million electric vehicles per year. However, these figures are still purely indicative and based on the study’s projections.
Vulcan estimates investment of €1.26 billion
Vulcan currently estimates the investment required for Ludwig at €1.26 billion, approximately 15 per cent lower than for Lionheart. The company attributes the reduced investment to lessons learned from the first project and the integration of lithium extraction and processing at a single location. Operating costs are projected at €4,101 per tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE). Vulcan places Ludwig in the lowest quartile of the global cost curve. However, these figures are also based on assumptions from its own pre-feasibility study and have yet to be confirmed by commercial operations.
Vulcan is significantly further along with Lionheart. For this first project, the company has secured financing of €2.2 billion and obtained construction permits for the facilities in Landau and Frankfurt-Höchst. Commercial production is scheduled to begin in 2028. Offtake agreements are in place with companies including LG Energy Solution, Umicore, Stellantis, and Glencore. In April, Vulcan also brought Siemens on board as a strategic investor and technology partner. According to the companies, the agreement will also extend to later development phases.
Ludwig, on the other hand, is still in a much earlier phase. Vulcan’s next steps include 3D seismic surveys, exploration drilling, and further technical development of the project. A final investment decision (FID) is not expected until after the successful start of production at Lionheart. The company has not yet specified a potential start date for production at Ludwig.
The project is also relevant in the context of Europe’s dependence on battery raw materials. According to a
Deloitte study
Vulcan itself is pursuing a long-term
expansion strategy in the Upper Rhine Valley
. Following the start of production at Lionheart, the company plans to develop additional projects at intervals of two to three years. Ludwig would represent the second phase of this plan. However, whether the project will actually be implemented in the form now outlined—and whether the assumed extraction volumes, investment, and operating costs will be achieved—will only become clear with further geological investigations and more detailed project planning..

title: China further reduces tax incentives for EVs - electrive.com
content:
Politics
China is gradually phasing out tax incentives for electric cars and batteries. Since September, the previously announced consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries has been in effect, and further benefits will be removed in 2027.
Lithium-ion batteries have been subject to a two percent consumption tax in China since September.
Image: BYD
Since 1 September, lithium-ion batteries have been subject to a consumption tax of two per cent. This will rise to four per cent in September 2027. The change was
already announced in July
and ends a tax exemption that has been in place since 2015.
In contrast, sodium-ion and solid-state batteries, as well as fuel cells, will remain exempt from consumption tax until the end of 2028. China is thus partially shifting tax incentives away from the now-established lithium-ion technology towards alternative technologies.
The immediate additional costs due to the new battery tax are likely to remain limited for the time being.
CarNewsChina
calculates that for an electric car with a 60-kWh battery, the two per cent tax would result in additional battery costs of around 438 yuan, or $62 USD. With the increase to four per cent, this would rise to around 876 yuan, or $125. However, the calculation is based on prices for Chinese LFP storage cells and is therefore merely an illustrative example.
The battery tax is just part of a broader realignment of China’s incentive policy: since the beginning of 2026, electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids (grouped under the NEV designation in China) have been subject to a
purchase tax
reduction of 50 per cent instead of a full exemption. The effective tax rate is thus five per cent, with the relief capped at 15,000 yuan per vehicle.
Furthermore, additional tax benefits for vehicle and vessel taxes are set to be abolished on 1 January 2027. These include battery-electric commercial vehicles, plug-in hybrids, range extenders, and fuel cell commercial vehicles. For purely electric passenger cars, however, this tax will remain unchanged.
China is thus gradually withdrawing from tax incentives that have supported the development of its NEV market for years. However, this does not mean the end of state support. Among other things, the state continues to invest in charging and battery-swapping infrastructure. In addition, the remaining tax benefits generally also apply to electric vehicles produced in China by foreign manufacturers.

title: UK firm hails onshore geothermal ‘lithium purity’ breakthrough – Batteries International
content: UK company Geothermal Engineering (GEL) has announced what it claims is a technological breakthrough in the production of onshore lithium in the country. GEL said on September 2 that independent analysis had shown the firm’s lithium carbonate produced from deep geothermal brine now exceeds the 99.3% purity specification — and can be classified as ‘technical grade’ material. The development at the United Downs site in Cornwall gives a direct route to market as the lithium carbonate does not need further refining before onward sale to battery manufacturers, GEL claimed. Production at the site started in February 2026 and GEL’s plant has a production capacity of 100 tonnes per annum of lithium carbonate. However, GEL said production at the site is now forecast to hit around 2,000tpa by 2029. As other sites are added, anticipated total production will increase to 30,000tpa by 2033, meeting over 60% of the UK’s lithium target alone, the company said. GEL’s CEO Ryan Law said: “We are demonstrating that it is possible to produce a high-quality, saleable lithium product in the UK with the highest environmental standards, creating the potential for a more secure and sustainable domestic supply of this critical battery material.” Julian Hetherington, director of automotive transformation at the Advanced Propulsion Centre, which is supporting the UK government’s Driving Research & Investment in Vehicle Electrification (Drive 35) programme, said: “United Downs shows the huge opportunity the UK has to build a domestic supply of lithium carbonate in a sustainable way. “It will strengthen the UK’s critical minerals supply chain and reindustrialise the country. Drive 35 is proud to have supported the project with a £1.8 million ($2.5 million) grant through our Automotive Transformation Fund, to help reach this important milestone.” The UK has set a target of meeting 10% of critical mineral demands from domestic production by 2035, including at least 50,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate. title: Range Rover Electric Combines Power and Luxury
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
The all-electric SUV combines luxury refinement with advanced traction control that responds 100 times faster than combustion models.
September 3, 2026
5 Min Read
The Range Rover Electric proves its mettle on the off-road course.
Jaguar Land Rover
At a Glance
The electric drivetrain produces 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque for a 4.3-second 0-60 time.
Traction control responds in 50 milliseconds, enabling superior off-road performance on steep slopes.
The 118.5-kWh battery charges from 10% to 80% in 22 minutes and provides 333 miles of EPA range.
Jaguar Land Rover brand
Range Rover
continues to position itself among the most premium luxury brands with the introduction of the
Range Rover Electric
, a model that is the quietest, smoothest, and quickest Range Rover to date.
It accomplishes these things while improving on the brand’s legendary off-road capability with an electric drive system whose traction management system responds 100 times faster than that on the
combustion-powered model.
In numbers, that means a combined 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque from its front and rear electric drive units, propelling the Range Rover Electric to 60 mph in just 4.3 seconds. It does this with a serene silence that is impossible in the combustion-powered model, with a sound level reduction of 7 decibels. “That’s the sound level of a living room versus a library,” Range Rover managing director Martin Limpert told
Design News
during a sit-down at the press launch.
The electric drivetrain is the key driver of the sound reduction, but as with other EVs, reducing drivetrain noise only showcases other noise sources. So, the Range Rover engineering team attacked wind noise through vehicle aerodynamic design and acoustic glass in the windows.
Our low-speed test drive on the JLR test track in Gaydon, England, wasn’t fast enough to reveal any high-speed wind or road noise, but it did confirm the Range Rover Electric’s utterly placid cabin environment at around-town speeds.
It is one thing to create a design with flush glass that can be made to work in theory and another thing for it to work in production, every time. Scanners check the part’s alignment at multiple spots on the assembly line, then in addition to the conventional water leakage test at the end of the line, Range Rover also checks for wind noise, according to chief engineer Lynfel Owen.
“We have some adjustments on the door glass to make sure it's truly fixed in a in a flush condition,” he noted. The mirrors were complicated by the A-pillar’s rearward position. “It brings that A-pillar into play with the wing mirror,” Owen observed.
“We had to put the wing mirror on the door,” he said. “When you do that without a [window] frame, you need to put more material and more stability into that door structure to stop the mirror moving, he said. “It might be small movements, but that sense of vibration goes into the body structure, and it gives you that feeling of something vibrating. So it's more costly, and it puts more structure into place, but it gives you elevated levels of refinement when you do it.”
Forget about fears of electricity and water, the Range Rover Electric is rated to handle 18 inches of water. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
As an EV, the battery technology and electric drive units are critical to the vehicle’s success. Range Rover is bucking the current trend toward piling cylindrical cells directly into the pack or even to the car’s body shell, as the 118.5-kilowatt-hour, 800-volt battery pack comprises 344 prismatic cells that are organized into modules.
The break from convention is that the cell’s contacts are on the sides rather than on the top, reducing the height of the battery pack. Rather than building the silicon carbide control electronics into the pack, they reside in a separate housing outside the pack.
The Range Rover Electric mounts the silicon carbide power electronics atop the pack in a housing shaped to fit into a conventional transmission tunnel. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
Range Rover says that the battery can charge to 80% state of charge from 10% in 22 minutes on a 350-kW charger, and the pack can split into two 400-volt packs for charging without voltage conversion on the more plentiful 400-volt charging stations. The EPA rates the driving range at 333 miles, and the charging port on US-market vehicles is the Tesla-style North American Charging Standard type.
On the trail, the Range Rover Electric delivers everything drivers expect from a Range Rover. That’s because the suspension provides the same 18 inches of wheel articulation as the combustion-powered version. And a wading depth of 35 inches combines with the ability to ascend 45-degree slopes.
Driving on Range Rover’s test track, we found that the Electric can not only climb steep slopes, it can cope with a slippery surface and obstacles like rocks and roots along the way. The traction control system can respond in just 50 milliseconds, making Range Rover Electric’s ability to handle treacherous conditions seem almost magical.
The Range Rover Electric's minimalist aesthetic might have too few physical buttons and knobs for some drivers' liking. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
Unlike in a combustion vehicle, there is no drama. For drivers who really use their billy goat vehicles for access to remote cabins and ski chalets rather than for tackling the Rubicon Trail, this is preferable because it doesn’t stress the driver or the passengers.
The ticket for admission for US customers starts at $138,000.

Discover why supply chain leaders are gathering in London on 8-9 September to navigate market turbulence and drive resilience with innovative strategies

Secure your ticket today

The core focus

The night will be exploring those who have adopted successful initiatives, or fostered innovation across the sector. The awards will also celebrate the most ground-breaking transformation projects and the companies which have integrated sustainability into their supply chains.
Co-located with The Global Sustainability Awards and The Global Procurement Awards, this night will be one recognition and inspiration.

Whether your focus is on modernising your supply chain with AI, integrating ESG policies, or nurturing budding partnerships across the value chain, the summit delivers key insights which can help you lead effectively.

title: Kaleris Acquires Newport to Automate M&R Supply Chains
content:
Kaleris Acquires Newport to Automate M&R Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Kaleris has announced its acquisition of Newport Systems, a leading provider of maintenance and repair (M&R) and depot management software. Credit Getty Images
Kirk Knauff, CEO of Kaleris, says the Newport Systems acquisition will accelerate its vision to deliver automation in maintenance and repair supply chains
Kaleris has announced its acquisition of Newport Systems, a leading provider of maintenance and repair (M&R) and depot management software.
It says the acquisition will create the industry’s only end-to-end M&R platform, connecting the full asset lifecycle across marine terminals, inland depots, rail terminals, equipment owners and repair providers onto a single platform.
Kirk Knauff, CEO of Kaleris, says: “The people and the technology network Newport adds accelerates our vision to
deliver automation
and optimisation at every critical node our customers depend on.”
Kirk Knauff, President and CEO at Kaleris. Credit: Kirk Knauff via LinkedIn
Why Kaleris acquired Newport Systems
Kaleris says the combined platform will be the only solution that spans the full intermodal ecosystem and the full range of assets, including containers, chassis, reefers, gensets and railcars, under a common M&R operating model.
Newport will add key expertise in M&R operations, pre-trip inspection workflows, reefer monitoring, genset management and temperature monitoring.
Kirk says: “Kaleris runs the most complex nodes in global trade, the terminal, the yard, the depot and maintenance is where value quietly leaks out of every one of them. Newport lets us close that gap.”
According to Kaleris, its reach across the most demanding segments of the supply chain has now been strengthened through Newport’s involvement.
One key factor behind Kaleris’ decision to acquire Newport is the company’s network of proprietary carrier and equipment owner integrations.
Newport has more than 20 years of industry relationships, including 25 live EDI integrations.
Key Facts Behind the Kaleris and Newport Systems Deal
25 - Live EDI integrations Newport holds
20 - Years Newport spent building industry relationships
5 - Asset types now covered under one model
4 - Node types connected on one platform
1 - End-to-end M&R platform created
Automating maintenance and repair
According to Kaleris, maintenance and repair is one of the least automated workflows in global logistics.
“We are automating the connection between the people who own the equipment and the people who repair it, replacing manual processes with work the system can carry," says Kirk.
Key companies
Headquarters: Alpharetta, US
CEO: Kirk Knauff
Kaleris is a leading provider of supply chain execution software specialising in transportation and yard management solutions. The business develops cloud-based operational technology for ocean terminals, rail networks, industrial shipping yards and trucking fleets. The organisation plays a critical role in global freight logistics, unifying multi-modal transport workflows, optimising asset tracking, reducing supply chain friction and enhancing visibility across complex international trade and distribution networks.
Newport Systems
Headquarters: Wall Township, US
CEO: Bob Morton
Newport Systems is an intermodal logistics technology provider delivering maintenance, repair and depot management software platforms. Serving ocean carriers, equipment lessors and container depots, the enterprise streamlines asset maintenance operations through its digital management tracking systems. The business plays an essential role in global shipping infrastructure by automating equipment inspection processes, managing repair estimates, improving fleet utilisation and standardising data exchanges across international supply chain networks.

title: Macfox X1S e-bike review: More mini-moto than bicycle, yet still street legal
content:
Micah Toll
| Sep 4 2026 - 8:37 am PT
There’s a fairly wide spectrum of moped-style electric bikes these days. Some are essentially conventional e-bikes wearing motorcycle-inspired designs, while others lean so heavily into the mini-moto experience that the pedals start to feel like little more than a legal technicality.
The Macfox X1S definitely falls closer to that second group.
After spending some time riding the bike, I don’t think this is the model I’d recommend to someone who actually enjoys pedaling. But if you want a fun little urban runabout with a motorcycle-inspired design, fat tires, and a right-hand throttle for cruising around at compliant 20 mph (32 km/h), and is street legal, then the X1S starts to make a lot more sense.
At $1,399
, the Macfox X1S is built around a 500W rear hub motor rated for 750W of peak power. Those specs are key, because along with the throttle on the handlebars, they help it fit just inside the Class 2 electric bicycle regulations used by most areas in the US. That keeps the bike street legal, even if it looks and feels more like a moped-style bike than anything else.
The Macfox X1S gets a 500Wh (48V 10.4Ah) removable battery, 20 x 4-inch fat tires, front suspension, hydraulic disc brakes, and a long bench-style saddle.
Macfox rates the single-battery model for up to 28 miles (45 km) of range, though there’s a dual battery version that gets twice the range.
That’s a pretty straightforward setup for this style of e-bike, with the exception that the battery is smaller than most you’d find on this style of bike.
But again, there’s that dual battery version, so if you’ve got an extra $299 burning a hole in your pocket, you can double up for twice the run time.
Going beyond the base specs, there are a couple of interesting details that help the X1S stand out.
First, as I mentioned, it’s a true Class 2 e-bike with a 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed. There are plenty of moped-style e-bikes out there that arrive capable of 30, 35, or even 40+ mph, putting them
well outside the legal e-bike classification
in most of the US.
The X1S doesn’t play that game. Macfox specifically markets it as Class 2 street legal, and the 500W motor is plenty for having fun around town without turning this into an e-motorcycle pretending to be an e-bike.
It may not crush hills the same way other models with twice the power can, but the smaller motor keeps the price lower and keeps the battery drain in check.
In my experience, cruising the urban jungle is really where the bike shines.
The X1S is just fun to zip around on. It has that little urban assault bike feeling where you can hop on, hit the throttle, and squirt around town like you’re on a miniature motorcycle. Sure, 20 mph isn’t going to rip your arms off, but on a small moped-style bike like this, it’s enough to put a smile on your face. Of course, “small” is relative. It’s a compact moped-style bike, but it still weighs a hefty 65 lb (29.5 kg).
And Macfox gets bonus points from me for putting the throttle on the right side – especially at a time when so many e-bike companies seem to be going insane and installing left-side throttles. Technically, the throttle is adjustable and removable, so theoretically you can reposition it, but having a right-hand throttle just feels more natural to me as someone who rides a lot of motorcycles and scooters.
It’s just the way the good lord intended two-wheelers to be. If they were supposed to have left-side throttles, they would have been born that way. (That’s a bit of sarcasm, before you blow up my comment section. But I still firmly believe in the virtues of right-side throttles, even if I support your right to choose. Get it? More sarcasm. I’ll be here all week, folks!)
Pedaling, on the other hand, isn’t exactly the X1S’s strong suit.
The bike has three pedal-assist levels and uses a cadence-based pedal assist system. Levels 1 and 2 aren’t overly jumpy, and I found them reasonably manageable. Kick it up into level 3, though, and the power comes on much more abruptly. At that point, there’s no mistaking this for a torque-sensor bike. You turn the pedals and the motor responds with a fairly binary-feeling shove. That’s a basic cadence sensor, through and through.
More importantly, the riding position simply isn’t conducive to effective pedaling. The long fixed-height bench seat and moped-style geometry leave the X1S borderline unpedalable in the traditional sense.
That isn’t universally true of this category. I’ve tested plenty of moped-style e-bikes that are surprisingly decent to pedal. The X1S just isn’t one of them.
So I quickly found myself treating those pedals more as auxiliary equipment and riding the X1S the way it seems to want to be ridden: with the throttle.
The component quality also generally matches the bike’s position in the market. You get front suspension rather than full suspension, and while it helps take the edge off rougher roads, don’t expect a particularly refined suspension setup.
The same goes for the hydraulic disc brakes. They work, and I’m glad to see hydraulic brakes here, but they didn’t have as much bite as I expected. It’s another reminder that simply reading “hydraulic disc brakes” on a spec sheet doesn’t tell you everything you need to know. Not all hydraulic brakes are created equal.
Fortunately, we’re dealing with a 20 mph e-bike here, not something that will be repeatedly hauling itself down from highway speeds. And over time the brakes did wear in a bit better, but still never got to where I’d prefer them, or where I get them to on higher end models.
There’s also some welcome news on the battery-safety front. Macfox says the X1S’s electrical system is UL 2849 certified, while the single battery is UL 2271 certified. Macfox notes that the dual-battery configuration falls outside the standard UL scope, an important distinction if you’re specifically shopping based on certification.
If you’re shopping for an e-bike because you love cycling and want something that enhances your pedaling, I’d look elsewhere. The X1S’s cadence sensor, geometry, and fixed bench seat simply aren’t designed around that experience.
If what you really want is a fun little 20 mph electric mini-moto that still fits neatly into the Class 2 e-bike framework, though, the Macfox X1S makes a much stronger case for itself. It’s simple, it looks cool, it’s fun to rip around on, and you can double the battery capacity if you want to spend more time cruising between charges.
Just think of the pedals as more of a supporting cast member than the star of the show.

title: Defender's smaller off-road EV spotted testing ahead of its debut
content:
Jaguar Land Rover
Range Rover
Peter Johnson
| Sep 4 2026 - 7:22 am PT
Defender is preparing to launch its first fully electric SUV, a compact off-roader that’s expected to debut by the end of the year.
When will Defender launch the Sport EV?
After the
Range Rover Electric
finally went on sale earlier this week, JLR is preparing to introduce its first EV under the Defender brand.
The electric SUV is expected to arrive in 2027, likely as the Defender Sport EV, and could make its official debut by the end of the year.
While the Range Rover Electric is fairly expensive, starting at £154,070 in the UK and about $140,000 in the US, the Defender “Sport” EV is expected to be positioned below the standard entry-level Defender SUV.
JLR has been talking about a “mini Defender” for years now, but it’s finally coming together. Ahead of its debut, expected later this year, a prototype was spotted testing around the Nürburgring.
Although it’s still disguised, the new spy images from
@Wilcoblok
reveal the Defender Sport EV will retain its signature boxy, rugged design in electric form.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by ᴡɪʟᴄᴏ ʙʟᴏᴋ (@wilcoblok)
It will also be just as capable, if not even more so with electric propulsion. Defender’s electric SUV will be the first to use JLR’s EMA platform, which will also underpin the upcoming Range Rover Velar EV.
The platform is expected to support battery packs ranging from 70 to 90 kWh, which should provide a range of at least 300 to 320 miles.
JLR’s EMA platform supports 800V fast charging and, although it was initially expected to be a dedicated EV platform, it will also support hybrid powertrains.
(Source: JLR)
Although it will be the brand’s smallest SUV and first EV, Mark Cameron, global managing director of Defender, told
earlier this year that the electric SUV will still feature the “epic, built-to-last, go anywhere capability” that Defender is known for.
As such, it’s expected to have a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain and JLR’s Terrain Response system.
Inside, it will feature a setup similar to the full-size Defender, but with larger display screens and a new user interface.
Defender 110 Trophy Edition (Source: Land Rover)
The Defender Sport EV, as it will likely be called, is expected to make its official debut by the end of 2026.
The sighting comes after Jaguar Land Rover’s CEO, PB Balaji, confirmed
during an investor update
in June that the company will focus on the Defender brand to drive growth in the US.
“Our aspiration, in the coming years, is to grow our US business to the size of the entire JLR business as it exists today,” Balaji explained.
JLR also recently announced a partnership with Jeep maker, Stellantis, to potentially develop and produce vehicles for the US. We should learn more soon. Check back for updates.

title: Tesla Full Self-Driving can now take over manual driving to avoid a collision
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Sep 4 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Tesla is rolling out a new version of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software that can take control of your car to avoid a crash, even when you’re driving manually.
The automaker announced the feature, part of FSD Supervised v14.3.9, in a post from its AI team early Friday.
FSD steps in even when you’re not using it
Tesla said v14.3.9 is “starting to roll out shortly” and includes what it calls “a new active safety feature set.” FSD Supervised “can now activate on your behalf when an imminent collision is detected and Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) may not be enough,” according to the company.
FSD Supervised v14.3.9 starting to roll out shortly
This release includes a new active safety feature set: FSD Supervised can now activate on your behalf when an imminent collision is detected and Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) may not be enough.
It may also engage if we…
Standard AEB brakes. This lets FSD take directional control and steer to avoid an obstacle when braking alone won’t cut it.
Tesla added that the system “may also engage if we detect you’re heavily distracted or have accidentally disengaged FSD.” So it can kick in two ways: an imminent collision that braking can’t solve, and moments when the driver looks checked out or FSD was switched off by accident.
A background safety net during manual driving
Until now, FSD only ran when you turned it on. A slice of the same
v14 software stack Tesla has been rolling out since April
now sits in the background while you drive manually, ready to intervene.
Tesla hasn’t said whether the feature can be turned off, or how it decides that steering is safer than braking. Those are big questions given the software’s record. We’ve documented v14
swerving toward a ditch for no reason
and Tesla’s long-running
phantom braking problem
in Autopilot. A false positive that brakes is jarring. A false positive that steers is a different level of risk.
Electrek’s Take
Automatic collision avoidance is a good idea in principle. AEB has prevented countless crashes, and letting the car steer around something it can’t brake for is a logical next step. Tesla isn’t alone here either; several automakers have been building evasive-maneuver systems for years.
But I hope it’s optional. AEB kicking in makes sense, and I want it – even though I use the most forgiving settings in my car because I think Tesla’s system is too aggressive. What I don’t want is FSD’s directional control taking over my steering when I’m in manual mode and have chosen to drive the car myself. Braking to save me is one thing. Deciding to grab the wheel and steer is another. If I’ve accidentally disengaged FSD, sure, catch me. I just want to know I can switch this off.
The bigger issue is trust. This is the same v14 that we’ve watched swerve for no reason and brake at phantoms, and now it’s cleared to act during manual driving. If Tesla gets the false-positive rate wrong, the feature could cause the exact crashes it’s meant to prevent.

title: Alliance for Automotive Innovation begs Congress to stop automotive innovation
content:
The entire US auto industry is back at it again, lobbying Congress to stifle competition and ensure that Americans remain stuck with overpriced, second-rate, highly-polluting vehicles.
The auto industry is rapidly moving towards electrification, and everyone knows it. This has been the case for more than a decade now, and smart countries and companies have worked to get themselves prepared for the future.
China is in this category, having prepared its auto industry for this moment by securing raw materials partnerships, supply agreements, production capacity, and a thriving EV startup culture – and contrary to the common story we’re told in the US, much of this preparation was bottom-up, rather than top-down. As a result, Chinese automakers are making some of the best, most affordable cars in the world right now, and the world is taking notice.
Then, there are the companies that seem desperate to lose, to sit on their laurels in a shrinking market and pretend that nothing is changing, and to beg for government to coddle them into feeling better about their poor decisions.
The US auto industry fits into the latter category, and John Bozzella, head of the main US auto lobby group the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (formerly known as Global Automakers), is king of the babies.
Chinese cars are already blocked, we need to block them again?
He pleaded with Congress on Thursday to pass multiple proposed bills banning Chinese vehicles from operating in the United States, despite that Chinese vehicles are already functionally banned from the US, in two different ways.
Not only is there a “connected car rule” (which Polestar just fell victim to), but there’s also a 100%+ tariff on Chinese EVs, making them simply uneconomical to sell in the US.
So as of yet, there has been little attempt to bring Chinese EVs to the US. Besides, why bother when the rest of the world wants them so badly, leading China to rapidly become the world’s #1 auto exporter, leapfrogging the US and 4 other nations that had held the top 5 for decades until the 2020s.
But that’s not enough protectionism for the free market capitalists in America, they must beg for government to coddle them further.
So Bozzella has now targeted the cowardly new effort in Congress that wouldn’t just ban the sale of Chinese EVs, it would ban Chinese EVs from even driving on American roads at all (e.g. if driven in from Canada or Mexico, two countries whose citizens are allowed to purchase these affordable, advanced vehicles).
In current form, it could also apply to companies with partial Chinese ownership, which would mean that Mercedes and Volvo would both be disallowed from operating in the US, though those and other provisions of the bills are subject to change.
Weren’t we told freedom and competition conquered all?
It’s an interesting strategy in a country whose mythos has always suggested that restrictive authoritarian regimes can be defeated by displays of “freedom.”
A common story in America goes that Soviets attempted to show American films to their people to highlight the depravity of American culture, but that the people instead saw the abundance of American life and were made jealous. The story is meant to show that freedom and cultural exchange can beat propaganda, and will lead to better outcomes for a populace.
Apocryphal or not, America is now on the other side of that story. At this very moment, Chinese cities are the most advanced in the world. Due to the abundance of cheap, clean electric transportation options, their air is clean and their streets are quiet. And their people have been the least negatively affected by the world’s oil-conflict-du-jour.
This lobbying only harms Americans’ health and pocketbooks
But John Bozzella and basically the entire US auto industry simply can’t have that. They’ve had it too good for too long, shoving gas-guzzling, child-killing SUVs down the throats of Americans, saddling everyone with more auto debt than ever, and ensuring skyrocketing war profits for their partner industry, oil.
All along, the auto industry has lobbied for more pollution. It does this even when it knows its a bad idea. It simply can’t help itself, it must try to harm the planet and even its own business prospects, as long as it will result in more gas being burned in America in the short term.
It’s a strange message coming from the “Alliance for Automotive Innovation,” where Bozzella has never found an opportunity to fight against innovation that he didn’t jump at.
The companies providing innovation in EVs, at this moment, are mostly focused in China. Automakers outside of China are stumbling all over themselves to cancel EV projects and push back targets, while China is just getting on with improving transportation.
They said Americans didn’t want EVs, now Americans want EVs too much?
After spending years pretending that Americans don’t want EVs and that government needs to roll back EV targets, and even losing themselves $70 billion seemingly for no other reason than to spite their face, Bozzella and the auto lobby are changing their tune.
Now they’re telling government that, no, Americans probably want EVs too much, well, at least Chinese EVs, and it’s totally not fair that China’s actually trying to make good EVs and we’re not and can you please ban them so we don’t have to try very hard pretty please?
Even the EVs that the US auto industry does make are overly large, overly expensive, and generally retrofit onto gas-vehicle designs that don’t properly leverage the advantages of EV powertrain packaging.
This is why the only EVs that sell well in America are those that were designed from the ground up to be electric, by a company that isn’t saddled with a century of combustible baggage.
Incidentally, these are the type of EVs coming out of China right now – clean sheet designs from startups that develop cars quickly and don’t have a parts bin of full of pistons and spark plugs they need to justify the existence of.

But protectionism hasn’t worked before, and it won’t work now. In the 1970s, the US saw an ascendant Japanese auto industry, with better processes and higher quality material inputs, and tried to stop it with tariffs. It failed to do so, but at least it bought itself some time to sit on its laurels and let Japan continue to improve, cementing them as a top auto exporter for the next half century.
The same story is playing out now, with China in the place of Japan. American Luddites like Bozzella are desperately trying to dig their heels into the ground and force a nation of 350 million people, who all have access to the internet, to close their eyes and stick their fingers in their ears and refuse to see what the rest of the world has access to.

title: Tesla Cybercab is already under NHTSA investigation after launch
content:
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 4 2026 - 5:46 am PT
Tesla’s Cybercab is already under federal investigation. NHTSA opened an audit into how Tesla certified the vehicle the same day the company started putting passengers in it in Austin.
The probe targets the exact thing that makes the Cybercab unusual: it has no steering wheel, no pedals, and no mirrors, and Tesla certified it as road-legal anyway.
Tesla launched the Cybercab commercially in Austin yesterday, and the event turned out to be the nothing-burger we
expected
. There was no livestreamed reveal, no stage presentation, and no public remarks from Elon Musk.
Instead, Tesla invited a small group of shareholders and friendly influencers to ride in the two-seater, with guests reportedly required to sign NDAs, before rides opened up more broadly through the Robotaxi app.
What NHTSA is investigating
The investigation is an Open Audit Query, numbered AQ26002, from NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation. It was “prompted by public information,” according to the filing, opened September 3, and it covers an estimated 1,000 Cybercab vehicles.
NHTSA says it’s examining “the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.”
Tesla told the agency it certified the vehicles as compliant with all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, and that it plans to gradually expand deployment to more vehicles and more locations.
The question is how Tesla got there. NHTSA says it will consider “the extent to which Tesla’s certification depended on determinations that certain FMVSS are inapplicable to the Cybercab.”
A car with no controls, self-certified
In the US, automakers don’t get their vehicles pre-approved by a regulator. They self-certify that a vehicle meets the federal safety standards, and NHTSA can investigate after the fact.
That system runs into a problem with the Cybercab. Many of the FMVSS were written around a human driver. They assume there’s a steering wheel, a brake pedal, side mirrors, and controls the driver can reach. The Cybercab has none of those.
Tesla’s answer was to decide that some of those standards simply don’t apply to a car with no human controls. Now NHTSA wants to see the work behind that decision.
This isn’t happening in a vacuum. Tesla’s driverless ambitions are already under a stack of federal scrutiny. NHTSA has an open probe into “Full Self-Driving” covering 3.2 million vehicles after a series of
visibility-related crashes
, and it collected crash data showing a
Tesla remote operator crashed a Robotaxi
earlier this year. The Cybercab runs on a very similar FSD software.
Electrek’s Take
Of course, this is an NHTSA investigation of Tesla, so like the Cybertruck launch, it’s more likely than not going to be another nothingburger.
Anyway, as we previously reported, Tesla is only going to deploy Cybercab in its limited geo-fenced robotaxi service. They won’t be sold to the public anytime soon.
In fact, Tesla is trying to pull another FSD and have fleet owners buy the Cybercab to deploy their own robotaxi services – shifting the burden to them. It’s going to be a mess.

title: South Korea to double 2027 budget for farm solar, agrivoltaics - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
South Korea plans to double government funding for factory rooftop solar and agrivoltaics to KRW 1.8 trillion ($1.3 billion) in 2027, as a new law regulating dual-use solar on farmland takes effect in December.
Brian Publicover
04 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Agrivoltaics
South Korea’s Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (MAFRA) has unveiled a 2027 budget proposal that includes expanded support for factory rooftop solar and agrivoltaics, while separate government budget materials indicate related spending will rise to KRW 1.8 trillion.
MAFRA Vice Minister Kim Jong-gu presented the ministry’s 2027 budget proposal of KRW 22.2215 trillion, an increase of KRW 2.0853 trillion, or 10.4% over the 2026 budget, in a briefing following a Sept. 1 Cabinet meeting.
According to associated government budget materials, funding for factory rooftop solar and agrivoltaics is set to rise from KRW 900 billion in 2026 to KRW 1.8 trillion in 2027.
Solar Income Villages program
, under which rural communities form cooperatives to install and operate solar plants on idle local land and share the resulting revenue, is set to expand from 700 to 2,200 villages, alongside a new guarantee scheme for the cooperatives. The same budget materials show KRW 1.4 billion allocated for agrivoltaics education and system-building to help farmers participate in the technology.
South Korea’s National Assembly passed the country’s first
dedicated agrivoltaics law in May
, along with amendments to South Korea’s Farmland Act, formalizing a legal framework for combining crop production and solar generation on the same land. The law, which takes effect Dec. 17, treats agrivoltaic installations as a temporary change of farmland use for up to 23 years and applies to self-cultivating farmers, tenant farmers, and resident-owned cooperatives.
Only the footprint of support structures is considered converted land under the law. The cultivated area beneath panels remains subject to farmland regulations. According to Seoul-based nonprofit Solutions for Our Climate, the law excludes zones covering nearly half of the country’s farmland.
Agrivoltaics deployment in South Korea remains at an early stage. Industry tracking of agrivoltaics projects identified 29 documented cases totaling approximately 12.4 MW of planned or confirmed capacity, with only about 537 kW verified as operating and roughly 1.3 MW at installation or completion stage as of August 2026.
The most advanced resident-led project is a 1 MW cooperative installation in Anseong, Gyeonggi province, which began construction in July. A larger
10 MW agrivoltaics array
is being developed as part of the 400 MW Haenam solar complex, South Korea’s largest single-site solar project to date, scheduled for completion in 2028.

title: Solar’s infrastructure obstacle - pv magazine Global
content: For years, the solar industry focused on lowering module costs, improving tracker technology, increasing inverter efficiency, and optimizing project financing. Those efforts transformed solar from a niche technology into one of the most competitive forms of new electricity generation in the world. Today, however, some of the most important variables affecting project schedules and economics have little to do with solar equipment itself. Transmission infrastructure, utility interconnection requirements, substation design, right-of-way complexity, and the availability of critical high-voltage equipment are becoming central to the future of energy development. Texas provides one of the clearest examples of this challenge. Driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, semiconductor production, and electrification, the state is experiencing unprecedented interest from both energy developers and large-load customers. What was once primarily a discussion about generation has increasingly become a discussion about infrastructure. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has received requests representing hundreds of gigawatts of prospective new load, much of it associated with data centers and large industrial customers. While not all these projects will materialize, the scale of the demand illustrates how rapidly the market is changing. Historically, developers often selected land first and addressed interconnection later. Today, that sequence is frequently reversed. Developers increasingly evaluate transmission availability, substation proximity, interconnection feasibility, voltage levels, and expansion potential before making final site selection decisions. Interconnection management Interconnection has become a strategic development discipline involving transmission planning, utility coordination, equipment procurement, permitting, land strategy, capital allocation, and long-term project scalability. Financial security requirements associated with interconnection can hit several million dollars before a project reaches financial close. Utility reviews may influence project schedules years before a facility begins generating electricity. Transmission upgrades can significantly impact both economics and timelines. These realities are reshaping the way projects are developed. Increasingly, successful developers must think like transmission planners. Site configuration, voltage selection, collector system design, future expansion capability, and right-of-way strategy are becoming critical decisions from the earliest stages of development. At the same time, an often-overlooked challenge is emerging within utility supply chains. Much of the industry’s supply-chain discussion over the past several years has focused on modules, batteries, and inverters. While these components remain important, a growing portion of schedule risk now resides within utility-controlled infrastructure. Transformers, breakers, switchgear, protection systems, relay packages, communication equipment, and substation components are increasingly determining project schedules. In one recent interconnection process, a utility-approved 345 kV breaker became one of the critical items for energization. While discussions often focus on modules, batteries, financing, and power prices, the availability of a single transmission component had a direct impact on project schedule and execution planning. From an investor perspective, this may sound surprising because it is usually the case that discussions around energy projects will focus on generation technology, financing structures, tax credits, and power prices. Yet the availability of a single high-voltage component can influence the timing of an entire project. Utilities understandably maintain strict qualification standards for critical infrastructure. However, problems inevitably arise if approved supplier pools become limited, causing decreasing procurement flexibility and increasing schedule risk. These are the types of challenges that rarely make headlines but increasingly shape project outcomes. This shift is particularly important because utility-scale solar and battery storage remain among the fastest generation technologies available. A utility-scale solar project can often be designed, financed, and constructed in less than two years, but the infrastructure required to connect that project to the grid may require significantly longer planning time frames. Electrification competition The energy industry often discusses artificial intelligence, data-center expansion, energy transition, and economic development as separate topics. In reality, these are converging to become parts of the same conversation. Every new data center ultimately becomes a generation, transmission, interconnection, and infrastructure challenge. Communities seeking to attract advanced manufacturing and large-load investments require confidence that sufficient power can be delivered when needed. Developers compete for access to transmission capacity. Utilities face growing pressure to expand infrastructure while maintaining reliability and affordability. The challenge extends far beyond renewable energy. This is a fundamental infrastructure challenge. The United States is entering what will likely become the largest electricity expansion cycle in generations. The industry’s ability to meet this future electricity demand will depend on much more than adding megawatts. It will depend on how effectively developers, utilities, regulators, equipment manufacturers, and investors work together to expand the infrastructure that supports those megawatts. The United States possesses the technology, capital, engineering expertise, and entrepreneurial ecosystem necessary to meet the challenge. The greater question is whether transmission systems, interconnection processes, and critical infrastructure supply chains can evolve quickly enough to support the unprecedented growth now being contemplated across the country. Over the past decade, the solar industry has demonstrated its ability to scale generation. The next decade will test its ability to scale the infrastructure required to deliver that generation where it is needed most. About the author Fernando Queiroz is CEO and executive director of engineering at Levona Renewables and founder of Infinite Photon. He has more than 18 years of experience in renewable energy, power infrastructure, and utility-scale project development across the Americas. His work spans engineering, EPC, interconnection strategy, transmission infrastructure, and project development, with a particular focus on large-scale energy infrastructure projects in ERCOT. title: Why agrivoltaics have yet to take off in Switzerland - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Agrivoltaics account for virtually none of Switzerland’s installed solar capacity, despite having the potential to generate far more electricity than the country currently consumes. A new ZHAW report identifies legal and administrative hurdles as key barriers and calls for regulatory reform, greater investment certainty, and lessons from neighboring markets.
Jochen Siemer
04 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
“Ground-mounted systems currently account for 0.1% of installed capacity, while agri-PV systems account for 0.0% (rounded).”
This sentence from a technical report by the ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences, essentially sums up the state of ground-mounted PV in Switzerland in general, and agri-PV in particular.
However, with the country’s Energy Act mandating an increase in renewable electricity generation, excluding hydropower, to 35 TWh per year by 2035 and 45 TWh by 2050, it will be difficult to continue excluding open-field sites.
In 2025, Switzerland’s 8.2 GW of installed PV capacity generated around 8.2 TWh of electricity. Meeting the country’s renewable energy targets, with PV expected to play a pivotal role, would require annual capacity additions of 2 GW to 2.5 GW.
The report notes that it remains an open question whether such volumes can be achieved “with the strong focus on rooftop installations, particularly because the potential of rooftop areas is not being exploited consistently enough under current legal frameworks and subsidy schemes.”
Potential: nearly twice Switzerland’s electricity consumption
The repot begins by outlining the technology’s advantages, which are much the same in Switzerland as elsewhere.
First and foremost is its enormous potential. The report estimates theoretical annual generation potential at 323 TWh. Even if installations are restricted to sites no more than 300 meters from the nearest grid connection point, the potential remains 113 TWh.
“This corresponds to nearly double Switzerland’s electricity demand in recent years and significantly exceeds the projected electricity demand in various net-zero scenarios,” the authors state.
Other drivers include potentially high profitability at suitable sites, the use of land with limited agricultural suitability, diversification of farm income, additional crop protection and climate adaptation benefits, as well as a positive public image and broad social acceptance.
On the latter point, agrivoltaics appear to enjoy greater acceptance than conventional ground-mounted solar – even in Switzerland, where opposition to ground-mounted PV tends to be considerably strong. At least, that is what the studies cited in the report suggest.
Legal hurdles are a key factor
At the same time, a lack of local acceptance is identified as a major obstacle to agrivoltaic projects. Other barriers include uncertain or insufficient profitability and potential restrictions on agricultural operations, particularly where large machinery is used.
Land ownership structures also play a role, as around half of Switzerland’s agricultural land is leased.
Taken together, however, legal and administrative barriers appear to be even more significant.
Article 24 of the Spatial Planning Act (RPG) is central to the issue. For PV installations on agricultural land, the rule is that solar use must not impair agricultural production. Instead, an installation must provide benefits for agricultural production or serve agricultural testing and research purposes.
That requirement alone goes a long way toward explaining Switzerland’s extremely small number of agri-PV installations.
The report cites a 2024 survey that identified 22 installations and estimates that the current total is “fewer than 100” – an estimate that itself appears optimistic. It assumes that these are “primarily research and pilot installations.”
Learning from neighboring countries’ mistakes
To change the situation, the report sets out a series of recommendations.
The first is to provide greater investment certainty, for example by adapting existing support mechanisms to the specific requirements of agrivoltaics. Another option would be to introduce a premium on top of the sliding market premium awarded through auctions, which has been available since 2025 but remains significantly underused. Similar premiums already exist for PV installations on parking areas and for systems with steep tilt angles, which deliver comparatively high winter electricity yields.
At least as important, however, is the report’s proposal to safeguard agricultural subsidy payments for land used for agri-PV, with the authors outlining a number of measures, most notably an amendment to Article 24 of the Spatial Planning Act.
Other recommendations include enabling and supporting local participation structures, such as citizen participation models and local energy cooperatives, as well as establishing dedicated advisory services.
The report also recommends translating national renewable energy targets into targets at the local level. While the cantons currently determine a large share of the legislation relevant to agrivoltaics, they are not required to meet specific capacity expansion targets.
Finally, the authors recommend learning from neighboring countries – and from the mistakes they have already made.
Germany, France, Italy, and Austria are described as being “significantly ahead of Switzerland in the development of agrivoltaics, both in terms of regulation and actual project implementation.”
“There is, therefore, an opportunity to bypass mistakes and focus directly on measures that work,” the report concludes.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Posco, BHP advance hydrogen reduction ironmaking technology - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, the Valencian government approved €76 million for BP-led renewable hydrogen and sustainable biofuel projects, while NaTran and Creos Deutschland started construction of the German section of the cross-border mosaHYc hydrogen network.
Meanwhile, Uniper completed the expressions of interest phase for its planned Wilhelmshaven hydrogen import terminal, which could ultimately handle 2.6 million metric tons of ammonia per year.
Sergio Matalucci
04 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Hydrogen
Posco’s Development Center housing the HyREX testing facility
South Korea’s
and Australia’s
have signed a collaboration agreement to advance Posco’s hydrogen reduction ironmaking technology, HyREX, following a memorandum of understanding signed in October 2025. HyREX combines hydrogen-based direct reduced iron (DRI) production using fluidized bed reactors (FBRs) with an electric smelting furnace (ESF) that melts the reduced iron. The HyREX process is designed to replace coal-based blast furnace steelmaking with hydrogen and electricity from renewable sources, reducing associated carbon dioxide emissions. Unlike many hydrogen-based ironmaking processes that rely on processed iron ore pellets, HyREX is designed to use fine iron ore directly. In the process, heated hydrogen passes through a series of fluidized bed reactors, suspending fine iron ore particles and removing oxygen from the ore. The reaction produces direct reduced hydrogen (DRI) and water vapor. The DRI is then transferred to an ESF, where it is melted and impurities are separated as slag. The ESF can process lower- and medium-grade iron ores, making the characteristics of the feedstock an important consideration. Under the collaboration, Posco and BHP will test BHP’s Australian fine iron ores to assess their suitability for the HyREX process, including their performance in fluidized bed reactors. The testing forms part of Posco’s plans to commercialize HyREX technology by 2030. “Under this agreement, Posco plans to verify the performance of HyREX technology in various raw material environments using BHP’s iron ore and strengthen the foundation for technology commercialization based on this,” said Posco.
Valencian government
has approved €76 million ($88.1 million) in direct grants for two projects led by BP and its subsidiary Castellón Green Hydrogen Phase 2. Of the total, €66.31 million will go to Castellón Green Hydrogen Phase 2 for a large-scale renewable hydrogen demonstration project, while BP Energía España will receive €9.7 million for a large-scale demonstration of advanced pretreatment technologies for sustainable biofuels, the regional government said. The funding will be distributed from 2026 to 2029, with €4.36 million allocated for 2026, €27.80 million for 2027, €34.07 million for 2028 and €9.78 million for 2029.
French gas transmission system operator
and Germany’s
Creos Deutschland
have started construction of the German section of mosaHYc, a cross-border hydrogen pipeline network. The approximately 17 km pipeline between Leidingen and Dillingen is the first hydrogen pipeline in the German state of Saarland. “After the final planning approval decision, the pipe and civil engineering work can now begin,” Creos Deutschland said, adding that construction is expected to take around 18 months.

The German energy company said the terminal’s modular design would provide an initial import capacity that could be expanded to a maximum annual throughput of 2.6 million metric tons of ammonia, equivalent to around 350,000 metric tons of hydrogen. title: TÜV Rheinland validates 4 kWh generation in Aptera’s solar electric vehicle - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Independent third-party testing measured more than 4 kWh of usable solar energy delivered post-conversion to the vehicle’s high-voltage battery.
Ryan Kennedy
04 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Cells & modules
Third-party testing from Germany’s TÜV Rheinland confirmed that Aptera Motors Corp.’s solar electric vehicle generated more than 4 kWh of usable solar energy daily across three test days in Southern California. The data provides a look at real-world vehicle-integrated photovoltaics (VIPV) under actual field conditions.
Vehicle solar has historically faced skepticism due to low panel tilt, shading, and limited surface area. However, the test results show how cell layouts and power electronics perform in the field. Testing logged energy delivered directly to the battery pack rather than estimating output at the module surface level.
Giorgio Bardizza of TÜV Rheinland conducted the on-site evaluation at Aptera’s Carlsbad facility. He used calibrated data logging equipment to track continuous generation from sunrise to sunset. Across three test setups, the vehicle’s 815.9 W peak photovoltaic system beat Aptera’s daily baseline target of 4.0 kWh.
A stationary test with the vehicle parked logged 4.23 kWh delivered to the battery. Turning the vehicle once at solar noon yielded 4.40 kWh. Opening the rear hatch toward the sun pushed delivery to 4.75 kWh. That translates to roughly 47 miles of daily range based on Aptera’s target efficiency rating of 100 Wh/mi.
The vehicle embeds 205 custom solar cells across seven distinct strings. These cells sit across four body zones: the hood, dashboard, roof, and rear hatch. Power logging across each string showed combined conversion losses between 9.2% and 9.6%. This indicates that sub-array efficiency remains steady under outdoor conditions.
As VIPV expands into commercial fleet and passenger markets, independent testing helps establish real performance metrics outside traditional solar arrays. Find the full
test report here

content:
Research & Development
Circular economy models encourage the extension of the lifecycle of both wind turbines and solar PV modules and the IEC is planning the appropriate standards.
International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
04 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Clusters of wind turbines and roofs covered with solar photovoltaic (PV) panels have become as familiar to most of us as electricity lines and poles. And it almost goes without saying how essential these installations are: solar and wind energy are fundamental in helping countries around the world achieve net zero emission targets.
But there is an environmental paradox which sits at the heart of our requirement for these renewables: when the equipment used to generate the energy reaches the end of its life, it becomes electronic waste (e-waste), unless it can be reused in other forms or for another purpose or its materials recycled. According to most experts working in the field, wind turbines have a lifespan of between 20 and 30 years. That means that there is a generation of wind turbines – a massive number of which were installed in the early 2000s – about to reach the end of its life. As IEC wind energy expert Alistair Mackinnon puts it in a previous
interview
, “Wind has become a mature and multi-billion industry, which is having to meet new challenges. One of them is the lifecycle of wind turbines.”
For solar panels, the lifespan can be longer and reach up to 40 years, according to some
estimates
. But even if they last longer, as some of the early models were manufactured before the noughties, end-of-life issues have to be addressed.
The problems with recycling solar modules
There are many regulatory incentives – notably the
directive in Europe – which attempt to stop countries from discarding e-waste in landfills or incinerating it. Despite this, this
UK company
which manages waste across the country estimates that approximately 350 million tonnes of e-waste is currently in landfills worldwide. And part of this e-waste is increasingly likely, at least in part, to come from crushed solar panels and discarded wind blades. One of the main problems is that some of the materials used for both renewable energy systems are difficult to recycle.
Solar panel cells are generally made of silicon. Glass, polymers and metals such as aluminium and copper are also part of the mix in the panel and the electronics used to make it work. While glass is relatively easy to recover and recycle, silicon is tricky. And as recycling targets are based on weight, it is easier to recycle the heavier glass components and ignore the lighter materials. As Tony Sample, the Chair of the IEC Technical Committee which prepares standards for solar PV systems,
IEC TC 82
, explains in this
: “It’s easy to meet targets by recycling aluminium frames, cables and glass. The difficult part is the module itself.”
It is also expensive: costs include transport to specialized recycling facilities, which are few and far between. Mechanical recycling is possible, such as using disassembled solar modules disintegrated into small pieces for road fill. This
’s activities include that type or recovery.
According to Secretary of TC 82 George Kelly, in this
interview
, companies specializing in that area “estimate that over 75% of a PV module can now be recycled thanks to innovative and high-performance processing and sorting techniques.”  More needs to be done to industrialize recycling processes, Kelly says, to bring costs down and make the business model viable.
The recycling challenge of wind rotor blades
Most problems arise with the materials used for the rotor blades of wind turbines. “Wind turbine blades are generally made of epoxy resin and other materials which are difficult to recycle,” Mackinnon admits. Epoxy resin is a thermosetting polymer which has many great properties, including mechanical strength, chemical resistance as well as thermal stability, but these properties are also what makes it virtually impossible to recycle as it cannot be melted.
New materials, particularly
thermoplastic composites
, which can be melted down to extract reusable resin, are now beginning to be used in the manufacturing process of turbine blades. Some new epoxy formulations are also designed to be recyclable. For existing epoxy resin blades, mechanical recycling solutions have included smashing the blades into small pieces for use in cement, concrete or fibre boards for flooring and walls. Some
companies
have specialized in that type of mechanical recycling, as with those involved in the repurposing of solar modules.
Repairing and using for longer: a cheaper and greener option
Circular economy models encourage the repair and longer use of electronic devices rather than their recycling, which is viewed as a last resort. Recycling is not only costly, but the process of recycling emits greenhouse gases and so does the transport to recycling facilities. The same analysis can be applied to solar panels and wind turbines. An IEC Publicly Available Specification (
), which is yet to be published, is expected to facilitate the repair and reuse of solar panels.
Kelly elaborates: “Our project team has been looking at several different scenarios and the most useful ways to address them. In one scenario, it is worth simply repairing the module for it to have a longer working life, because the repair is easy to make and not too costly. In another scenario, the system may need replacing but the module itself is perfectly fine and can be used for a second life in remote and poor communities who can’t afford to install the most recent tech. And a third one is about recycling the materials in the system.”
The same thinking is taking place in
IEC TC 88
, the technical committee which prepares standards for wind energy systems. In 2025, the TC published
IEC 61400-28
, which sets out the minimum requirements to extend the life of wind farm assets in a safe manner. It is included in
, (IEC System for Certification to Standards Relating to Equipment for Use in Renewable Energy Applications), which is working on an operational document on the life extension of wind turbines. IECRE is the most recent of the four IEC Conformity Assessment Systems and focuses on providing third party certification and testing services for all power plants producing, storing, or converting energy from wind, marine and solar PV energy.
“The idea is to ensure that wind turbine assets that are used beyond their initial lifecycle still perform safely and efficiently. By working hand in hand, experts from TC 88 and IECRE can promote the idea of a more circular economy in the wind sector,” says IECRE Secretary Wolfram Zeitz.
The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) is a global, not-for-profit membership organization that brings together 174 countries and coordinates the work of 30.000 experts globally. IEC International Standards and conformity assessment underpin international trade in electrical and electronic goods. They facilitate electricity access and verify the safety, performance and interoperability of electric and electronic devices and systems, including for example, consumer devices such as mobile phones or refrigerators, office and medical equipment, information technology, electricity generation, and much more.

title: New energy products emerge in Southern Africa’s renewables market - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The final article in a series on energy markets in Southern Africa explores how the liberalisation of the region’s electricity markets is bringing a shift from purely selling variable electricity towards products that are tailored to specific customer and system needs.
Patrick Jowett
04 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Utility-scale
Southern Africa’s renewable energy market appears to be entering a new phase, with companies increasingly looking to package solar, storage and flexibility into products designed around specific customer needs.
Dominic Goncalves, Advisory Partner for Energy Strategy at Cresco Project Finance and Founder & Director of Naviara Energy, told
pv magazine
that the next race in Southern Africa’s renewable energy market will be to transform variable electricity into differentiated products that solve specific customer needs and system problems.
“Firming is the monetisation of variability: it converts electricity generated when the resource is available into a product delivered when the customer or power system values it most,” Goncalves explained.
“Customers in Southern Africa rarely want the uncontrolled output of an individual renewable plant, they want a solution to a specific energy problem,” he added. “In 2026, there is an emerging product development opportunity and redesigning of commercial strategy towards what customers want, how those products are constructed and which companies may capture the value.”
Adding value to solar
Goncalves said a combination of changing market dynamics, including ongoing market liberalization, and technological advancements have created the conditions for Southern Africa to adopt more tailor-made products.
“We can now bridge the gap between what customers want and what people in the renewable energy business are able to achieve by using solar and wind as the main anchors and then bolting on additional services that create products and contracts that reflect added value,” he explained.
Customers are looking for solar to be dispatchable, predictable and shaped according to demand, Goncalves added.
“While a mine in Southern Africa typically wants reliable, competitively-priced baseload supply and reduced diesel dependence, a manufacturer in the region wants a shaped profile matching its operating hours and protection from peak prices while a data centre will be looking for high availability, measurable renewable matching and energy security,” he said.
Such considerations increasingly involve designing the physical and contractual solution backwards from the customer’s requirement.
“Buyers now value timing, shape, flexibility, reliability and contractual choice,” Goncalves added. “The next competitive advantage lies in designing and delivering those products.”
Goncalves also warned that companies who are unable to provide firmed or flexible power could increasingly find themselves pushed out of the market.
“Companies that continue to develop an asset first and search for an offtaker later may find that they have produced unwanted electricity, during the wrong hours, at the wrong location or with the wrong risk profile,” he explained. “Meanwhile, the rewards will be reaped by those who are able to provide firming value: converting intermittent renewable energy into predictable delivery profiles, dispatchable output and contractually guaranteed supply.”
Developing business models
Emerging business models in Southern Africa including subscription fees, availability payments, as-a-service models, PPA premiums, tolling arrangements and profit sharing, Goncalves explained.
While some of these are viable for implementation already, others require further market development, for example under the planned South Africa Wholesale Electricity Market implementation and existing South African Power Pool.
“However in some cases, first movers – for example in ancillary services and flexibility services – may help create those markets by translating an unmet system need into a measurable and buyable product,” Goncalves added.
Virtual power plants (VPPs) represent one of the clearer near-term product opportunities in Southern Africa, Goncalves continued, particularly for aggregating commercial, industrial and residential batteries, embedded generation and flexible demand. Elsewhere, demand-side management, industrial load reduction and forecasting, and optimisation software are key opportunities to address, particularly for industrial and mining customers in Southern Africa.
Goncalves suggested that one of the largest undeveloped product opportunities may sit at the intersection of transmission congestion and curtailment.
“Southern Africa still lacks widely adopted commercial products that combine storage, portfolio substitution and contractual risk allocation to protect buyers and generators when otherwise-available electricity cannot be delivered,” he explained.
New opportunities
Goncalves told
pv magazine
that the competitive landscape of renewable energy companies successfully operating in Southern Africa could look quite different by 2030.
“[These companies] are unlikely to be simply project developers, IPPs or traders,” he said. “There is an increasing pool of companies that are currently creating new types of products to address new types of needs, while progressive project developers, IPPs or traders embark on developing new products themselves.”
This shift, alongside the growing complexity of multi-technology solutions, opens new opportunities for entrepreneurs and companies to develop new products and solutions, Goncalves said, while new partnerships are expected to be key to successfully rolling out such products across the region.
“There are opportunities for partnerships because many of the solutions are complex, requiring multiple technologies and skills spanning different backgrounds,” he explained.
“One company may find it hard to develop an entire product offering in-house and may seek to partner to fill gaps. Meanwhile, there is international precedent to some of these products and solutions – international players would require local partners to successfully execute and roll-out product in Southern Africa, while local companies could draw on international experience as they localise and adapt those products for the local market and specific customers in the region.” Goncalves added.
“There’s plenty of space for everyone to take a look at solar and start to provide layers of value on it.”
Previous articles in this series covered the factors that are turning Zambia into
one of Africa’s most attractive markets
for renewable energy investment, the
liberalization of Southern Africa’s electricity markets
death of the traditional power purchase agreement
in the region.
